prompt: `no_sdk.py` opened a span with only the API installed. What did it record?
hint: Look at the trace id it printed.

choices.text: An error saying no SDK was configured
choices.why: The API never raises for this; silence is its design.

choices.text: Nothing: a non-recording span with a zero trace id
choices.why: Right. Without an SDK the API hands back spans that do nothing, cheaply.

choices.text: A span kept in memory until an SDK is installed later
choices.why: Nothing is kept; there is nowhere for it to go.

choices.text: A span printed to the console by default
choices.why: Printing needs the console exporter, which is part of the SDK.

prompt: Why is it useful that the API alone records nothing?

choices.text: It makes spans faster to read in a backend
choices.why: No span reaches any backend.

choices.text: It lets the SDK be installed without restarting
choices.why: The SDK is set up when the program starts.

choices.text: A library ships its instrumentation to people who never set OpenTelemetry up, at almost no cost to them
choices.why: Right. The calls stay in the library and cost nearly nothing until someone installs an SDK.

choices.text: It keeps personal data out of traces
choices.why: Whether a span records has nothing to do with what is put in it.

prompt: Match each SDK piece to its job.

pairs.right: Creates real spans, and carries the resource
Decides when a finished span is exported
Says who produced the spans, such as `service.name`

right_distractors: Chooses which spans the backend shows first

prompt: The resource attribute every backend groups spans by is `service.___`.
The team decides to send traces to a different backend. What has to change in the storefront's checkout code?
hint: The checkout code uses only the API.

choices.text: Nothing
choices.why: Right. Where spans go is the SDK's configuration, set once at start-up.

choices.text: Every `start_as_current_span` call
choices.why: Those are API calls and are the same whatever the backend.

choices.text: The attribute names, to match the new backend
choices.why: Semantic conventions are shared by every backend.

choices.text: The `kind=SpanKind.SERVER` argument
choices.why: The kind describes the work, not the destination.

prompt: In `first_span.py`'s output, `parent_id` is `null`. What does that make the span?

choices.text: A span that failed to export
choices.why: It exported: it is printed.

choices.text: The root of its trace
choices.why: Right. A span with no parent is where its trace begins.

choices.text: A span from another service
choices.why: A remote parent would still be a parent id.

choices.text: An internal span the backend will hide
choices.why: `INTERNAL` is its kind, and nothing is hidden.

prompt: The span started at `03:33:35.497358` and ended at `03:33:35.497481`. How many microseconds did it last?
Why are trace and span ids random rather than numbered in sequence?
hint: Who would hand out the next number?

choices.text: Random numbers compress better in storage
choices.why: They compress worse, if anything.

choices.text: So that nobody can guess how many orders the shop takes
choices.why: That would be a side effect, not the reason.

choices.text: The W3C forbids counters in headers
choices.why: There is no such rule.

choices.text: Every process can start traces without asking anyone else for a number
choices.why: Right. A counter would need one place to hand out numbers, and every service would depend on it.

prompt: Nobody set `service.instance.id`, yet the resource carried one. What is it for?
hint: There can be more than one copy of a service.

choices.text: Telling apart two running copies of the same service
choices.why: Right. The SDK generates one per run of the program.

choices.text: Linking the span to its parent span when that parent runs in another service
choices.why: Parents are linked by span ids, not by the resource.

choices.text: Identifying the machine's operating system
choices.why: That would be other resource attributes, which this script did not set.

choices.text: Counting how many spans the process has made
choices.why: It is an id, not a count.

prompt: In `nested.py`, `price()` never receives the basket's span. How does each lookup end up as its child?

choices.text: The tracer remembers the last span it created
choices.why: It uses the current span, not the last one created; a finished span is not a parent.

choices.text: The basket's span is current while `price()` runs
choices.why: Right. `start_as_current_span` takes the current span as parent.

choices.text: The exporter rebuilds the tree from start times
choices.why: The parent id is set when the span starts, not guessed later.

choices.text: Python passes the parent implicitly, as a hidden argument to every function
choices.why: There is no hidden argument; the current span lives in a context variable.

prompt: The console printed the two lookups before the basket. Why?

choices.text: The console sorts spans by span id
choices.why: The ids are random; no sort is applied.

choices.text: The basket was exported late because it was larger
choices.why: Size has nothing to do with it.

choices.text: A span is exported when it ends, and the basket ended last
choices.why: Right, which is why a backend must rebuild the tree from ids and never from arrival order.

choices.text: Child spans always have a higher priority than their parents in the processor
choices.why: Processors have no priorities.

prompt: The two lookups took 10.2 ms each and the basket 20.7 ms. How many milliseconds of the basket were spent outside both lookups?
A service handles each request by handing the work to a new `threading.Thread`. Spans created in that thread appear as roots of new traces. What happened?
hint: What does a new thread start with?

choices.text: The SDK refuses to record from more than one thread
choices.why: It records from any thread; the parent is what went missing.

choices.text: The new thread started with no current span, so nothing was there to be the parent
choices.why: Right. The context has to be handed to the thread explicitly.

choices.text: The batch processor reorders spans across threads
choices.why: Order does not decide parents; ids do.

choices.text: Threads get a new `service.instance.id`
choices.why: The resource belongs to the process, not the thread.

prompt: Which attribute belongs to OpenTelemetry's semantic conventions rather than to the shop?
hint: Which one would any web service use?

choices.text: `shop.sku`
choices.why: The `shop.` prefix marks the shop's own.

choices.text: `http.route`
choices.why: Right. It means the same thing in every service and every backend.

choices.text: `shop.total_cents`
choices.why: A shop attribute; no convention knows about totals in cents.

choices.text: `shop.quantity`
choices.why: Again the shop's prefix.

prompt: Why do the shop's own attributes start with `shop.`?

choices.text: Jaeger only stores an attribute whose name starts with a prefix of some kind
choices.why: It stores any key.

choices.text: Prefixed attributes are indexed for search
choices.why: A prefix changes nothing about indexing.

choices.text: So that a convention published later never clashes with them
choices.why: Right. `sku` alone could one day mean something else in somebody else's convention.

choices.text: The prefix encrypts their values
choices.why: A name encrypts nothing.

prompt: Which of these should never be set as a span attribute? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: The card number from the request body
choices.why: Yes. A trace is stored, shipped and read widely.

choices.text: The session token from a header
choices.why: Yes. Anyone reading the trace could use it.

choices.text: The order id
choices.why: An id is safe and is exactly what makes one order findable.

choices.text: The product's SKU
choices.why: A product code carries nothing personal.

choices.text: The customer's password
choices.why: Yes, never, anywhere.

prompt: Why can a span carry an order id as an attribute when lesson 6 warns against an order id as a metric label?
hint: What does each extra value cost?

choices.text: Attributes are dropped by the Collector, labels are not
choices.why: The Collector forwards attributes.

choices.text: Spans are sampled, so ids never accumulate
choices.why: The lab keeps every span; sampling is not the reason.

choices.text: A span is stored once whatever its values; a label value makes a new series that lives on
choices.why: Right. That is why high cardinality belongs in attributes.

choices.text: Metrics cannot hold numbers above a million
choices.why: Values are not the problem; distinct label values are.

prompt: Which call marks the storefront's span as failed?

choices.text: `span.set_status(Status(StatusCode.ERROR, ...))`
choices.why: Right. Backends turn that into `error: true`.

choices.text: `span.record_exception(e)`
choices.why: That adds an event with the exception; it does not by itself mark failure.

choices.text: `log.error(...)`
choices.why: A log line is a separate signal.

choices.text: `return {"error": ...}, 503`
choices.why: The response code reaches the customer; the span's status is set separately.

prompt: What is a span event?

choices.text: A child span with no duration
choices.why: Events are not spans and have no id.

choices.text: A log line copied into the trace by Loki
choices.why: Loki stores logs; it does not write into traces.

choices.text: A timestamped note inside a span
choices.why: Right, with attributes of its own, like the exception's type.

choices.text: An alert raised from a failed span
choices.why: Alerts come from rules, lesson 5 onward.

prompt: The storefront answers `404` for an unknown product. Following OpenTelemetry's HTTP conventions, which span is marked as an error?

choices.text: Both the client's and the server's
choices.why: That is the rule for a `5xx`.

choices.text: Only the server's, because it refused
choices.why: Refusing correctly is the server doing its job.

choices.text: Only the client's, if the client is instrumented
choices.why: Right. A `4xx` is the caller's failure; the server's status stays unset.

choices.text: Neither, because `404` is not a failure for anyone
choices.why: It is a failure for the client that asked for something that does not exist.

prompt: `cost.py` exported 2000 spans in 1.85 s with the simple processor and 0.08 s with the batch one. Where did the simple processor's extra time go?

choices.text: Compressing each span before sending
choices.why: Compression is not what differs between the two.

choices.text: An HTTP round trip to the Collector inside every `with` block
choices.why: Right: the code waited for the network once per span.

choices.text: Creating 2000 threads, one per span
choices.why: Neither processor creates a thread per span.

choices.text: Retrying spans the Collector refused
choices.why: Nothing was refused.

prompt: A service using the batch processor is killed with `kill -9`. Which statements are true? Choose all that apply.
hint: Where are spans waiting between sends?

choices.text: Spans still in the queue are lost
choices.why: Yes. Nothing runs after a `kill -9`.

choices.text: The lost spans are from its last seconds
choices.why: Yes, often the ones that would explain the death.

choices.text: The SDK's exit handler flushes them first
choices.why: Exit handlers run on a normal exit, not on `kill -9`.

choices.text: The Collector asks the process for its unsent spans
choices.why: The Collector only receives; it never pulls from a service.

prompt: The environment variable that tells the OTLP exporter where to send is `OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP____`.
The Collector stops answering for ten minutes. What does the Python batch processor do with new spans?

choices.text: Keeps every span in memory until the Collector returns
choices.why: That would grow without limit and could take the service down.

choices.text: Blocks each request until there is room
choices.why: Telemetry never holds up the service.

choices.text: Keeps up to its limit and drops the rest
choices.why: Right: 2048 by default. Losing telemetry is the right failure.

choices.text: Writes them to a file and sends them later
choices.why: The SDK has no disk queue.

prompt: Fifty orders produced fifty operations in Jaeger. Which name would have produced one?

choices.text: `GET /orders/1011`
choices.why: That is the problem: the id is in the name.

choices.text: `GET order 1011 for kettle`
choices.why: Still a value in the name.

choices.text: `GET /orders/{id}`
choices.why: Right, with the id in an attribute.

choices.text: `GET /orders/` plus a random suffix
choices.why: Any per-request part multiplies the names.

prompt: Put the consequences of naming spans with the order id in the order they appear, from the first span to the bill.
hint: Start in the list of operations.
items: Each order adds an operation to the service's list
Filtering by operation becomes searching for one order
Metrics computed per operation get one series per order
The bill for series grows with every order

prompt: A span's name says what kind of work it is; its ___ say which instance of that work it was.
